metadata.title: Claude, Investigation Add.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude gain authority to open a workplace investigation when it picks up the investigation-add skill? Lands the carry-out that a skill is a checklist Claude reads before it starts, not new decision-making power.

beats.narration_text: Read the name investigation-add and it sounds like Claude opens the case. It logs one. Inside that folder is a single file — that's what actually runs. Let's take it apart.

beats.narration_text: Hear "Claude has an investigation-add skill" and the intuitive read is: Claude opens the case. It decides when the investigation starts. That's what the name is optimized to sound like — and it's wrong.

Here's the falsification. Delete the folder and nothing inside the model shifts. No investigative authority is lost, because none was ever granted. What Claude actually loses is one checklist for logging a new case — that's the whole subtraction.

Here's what a skill actually is: one file. Investigation-add is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — plain-language instructions for logging a new workplace investigation, step by step. Claude reads that file before it does anything else. That's the whole mechanism — a document, not a model change.

The execution model is deliberately boring. Claude reads the file top to bottom and works through it in written order. No branching unless the file itself says branch. Predictability is the design choice — same steps, same sequence, every run.

That makes a skill a specification, not new judgment — they optimized for uniform intake at the expense of situational insight. The payoff: the same intake, every investigation, every time. The limit: step outside those written steps and Claude has no special opinion about it.

So investigation-add never handed Claude authority to open a case. What it guarantees is different — every run reads the same file, logs the case the same shape. Repeatability, not power. That's the whole trick.

beats.narration_text: Now the honest part — two failure modes the design accepts. A fully filled record doesn't prove Claude judged the situation correctly; a checklist followed to the letter can still miss what it was never asked to check. And a blank field doesn't prove nothing's wrong; it can just mean this case is outside what the checklist covers.

A skill named investigation-add doesn't hand Claude authority to open or judge a case — it's a checklist Claude reads before it starts. Same intake every time. Anything outside those steps is still on you.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want a Claude skill for one workplace record I fill out the same way every time — an incident log, an intake form, a status update. Write me a SKILL.md for it: plain language, ordered steps, no branching unless a step explicitly says to branch. Include the exact fields Claude should ask about, in order, using the phrasing Claude should read back to me. Then name two situations this checklist would definitely miss — cases where the fields don't cover what actually matters. Go deeper: take one of those missed situations and write me the second SKILL.md that catches it, and tell me where the two skills should hand off to each other.
